# Waves - sound and light (`wave_nature_light_sound`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by air_pump_vacuum, refraction_optics, spectrum_colour
- Core idea: Sound is a back-and-forth vibration passed on through air (or water, wood, metal) as a wave; nothing travels but the disturbance. It moves about 340 m per second in air, so three seconds between lightning and thunder mean one kilometre. Pitch is the number of vibrations per second; halving a string doubles it and gives the octave. A bell in a jar pumped empty of air falls silent. Light also behaves as a wave, with an extremely short wavelength (about half a thousandth of a millimetre): light from one source passing through two very close slits makes bright and dark stripes, because waves from the two slits add in some places and cancel in others. Colour is wavelength, red longest.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying sound and light are the same kind of wave: sound needs a medium, light crosses a vacuum
  - Insisting on a light-carrying ether (assumed until 1905, never detected)
  - Double-slit demonstration fails with a wide source or slits more than a fraction of a millimetre apart
  - Claiming light is 'only' a wave; since 1905 it is known to come in quanta as well
- History: greece: 6th c. BC – Pythagorean string ratios (the hammer story is legend); 4th c. BC Aristotle, later Vitruvius, compare sound to ripples; china: c. 3rd c. BC – tuned bells and pitch pipes with numerical rules; 1584 Zhu Zaiyu computes equal temperament; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Farabi and Ibn Sina on sound as air in motion; europe: 1636 Mersenne's laws of strings and a measured speed of sound; 1660 Boyle's bell in vacuum; 1665 Grimaldi describes diffraction; 1678–1690 Huygens' wave theory; 1801–1803 Young's interference experiments; 1815–1821 Fresnel; 1865 Maxwell: light is an electromagnetic wave
- Read:
  - Christiaan Huygens, Traité de la lumière (1690)
  - Thomas Young, Experiments and Calculations Relative to Physical Optics, Philosophical Transactions 94 (1804)
  - Jed Z. Buchwald, The Rise of the Wave Theory of Light (1989)
